explain.say: The petrol in a car, the gas in a cooking cylinder and the tar on the road all come from one black liquid: crude oil! It is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons. Look at the board. You can see a tall tower that sorts them out.

faq.q: What is each fraction used for?
faq.a: Refinery gas is bottled for cooking, petrol fuels cars, kerosene fuels jet planes, diesel fuels lorries and trains, fuel oil powers ships, and bitumen surfaces roads.

faq.q: Why do long chains collect at the bottom?
faq.a: Longer hydrocarbon molecules have stronger forces between them, so they have higher boiling points. They condense in the hot bottom of the tower, or never boil at all.
asks: Why does bitumen come out at the bottom?

faq.a: Crude oil is heated until most of it boils. The vapour rises up a tower that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top, and each fraction condenses at the level that matches its boiling point.
asks: Explain fractional distillation of crude oil

faq.a: A hydrocarbon is a compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only. Crude oil is mostly hydrocarbons, from tiny methane to huge chains in bitumen.

faq.q: Why is crude oil called a fossil fuel?
faq.a: It formed over millions of years from the remains of tiny sea creatures buried under mud and rock. It cannot be replaced once used, so it is non-renewable.

facts: Crude oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, separated by fractional distillation into fractions with similar boiling points.
Shorter-chain fractions have lower boiling points, flow more easily and catch fire more easily than longer-chain fractions.
